The Ruff (Calidris pugnax) exhibits a fascinating life history shaped by its lekking mating system and long-distance migratory ecology. At hatch, downy chicks emerge weighing approximately 10 grams [Wwb = approximately 10 grams], a mass that supports rapid thermoregulatory development in arctic breeding grounds. Egg incubation periods are tightly linked to nest temperature regimes; at an average incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the age at birth or hatching requires 21 days [ab = 21 days]. This duration reflects the energetic constraints of maintaining egg warmth in the variable tundra climate, where attending adults must balance foraging bouts with constant nest attendance. The relatively small initial body mass (10 grams) is consistent with the precocial developmental mode typical of many calidridine sandpipers, enabling chicks to leave the nest and begin self-feeding within hours of hatching. However, complete independence is not immediate; the nestling period, though brief, involves sustained parental brooding to supplement the chick's limited thermoregulatory capacity.

Under the active metabolic body temperatures characteristic of this species, approximately 41 °C [T = 41 °C], fledging occurs at a remarkably early 9 days after hatching [tx = 9 days after hatching] and puberty is attained at 27 days after hatching [tp = 27 days after hatching]. This rapid transition from nest-bound chick to flight-capable fledgling is an adaptation to the short arctic summer, allowing young birds to escape nest predation and begin accumulating energy reserves before autumn migration. The ability to achieve flight so quickly is supported by intensive biparental care during the first week post-hatch. As the fledgling matures, sexual maturation proceeds over a longer time frame; this relatively early puberty for a shorebird allows individuals to achieve reproductive readiness within their first summer, though actual breeding is deferred in most cases due to the demands of migration and territory establishment.

Reproductive output in the Ruff is comparatively modest, reflecting the high energetic investment required for long-distance migration and male-male competition on leks. Annual reproductive effort is limited to a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], meaning that successful pairs produce just one brood during the brief breeding season. Within this single annual breeding event, the maximum clutch size typically recorded is 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 eggs per clutch]. The timing of the first reproductive event is also tightly constrained by the migratory schedule. Under the thermal conditions of the active metabolic state (41 °C [T = 41 °C]), the time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days]. This indicates that most individuals defer their first breeding attempt until their second calendar year, following a complete annual cycle of migration, overwintering, and return to the breeding grounds.

Striking sexual dimorphism is a defining feature of Ruff life history, particularly in adult body size and mass. The ultimate wet weight or adult asymptotic body mass for females reaches approximately 110 grams [Wwi = approximately 110 grams], a figure consistent with the female's role as the sole incubator of the clutch. In marked contrast, males achieve a substantially larger ultimate wet weight of 180 grams [Wwi = 180 grams], a difference driven by sexual selection for larger body size and ornamental plumage that enhances success on the lek. This size disparity, with males being over 60% heavier than females on average, is among the most pronounced in the shorebird family Scolopacidae. The additional mass in males supports the development of the elaborate neck ruff and head tufts that are displayed during courtship, as well as the physical stamina required for prolonged agonistic interactions at the lek arena. These body mass values, 110 grams [Wwi = 110 grams] for females and 180 grams [Wwi = 180 grams] for males, represent the upper asymptote of post-juvenile growth and are typically attained by the end of the first year of life.

Longevity in the Ruff is considerable for a shorebird of its body size, reflecting a slow pace of life that balances high adult survival with low annual reproductive output. The maximum documented lifespan in the wild, recorded through re-sightings of color-ringed individuals, reaches 19.9 years [am = 19.9 years] at the active body temperature condition of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This extended lifespan, approaching two decades, allows individuals multiple opportunities to breed across their lifetime, partially offsetting the limitation of only one clutch per year. Such a longevity value places the Ruff among the longer-lived members of the Charadriiformes order, comparable to other arctic-breeding shorebirds that face high migratory costs but low predation pressure during the breeding season. The ability to survive for nearly 20 years under natural field conditions is a testament to the species' robust physiological capacity for withstanding the energetic extremes of biannual transcontinental migrations, which impose substantial metabolic demands at the elevated body temperatures typical of active flight.
